passages.t: ‘O God of vengeance, shine forth’: justice for the widow and the fatherless
passages.happening:
Psalm 94 has no heading. It opens with a hard name for God: “O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth” (verse 1). “Rise up, O Judge of the earth” (verse 2).

Then the complaint. “How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?” (verse 3). They crush God's people (verse 5). “They kill the widow and the foreigner; they murder the fatherless” (verse 6). And they think no one is watching: “The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed” (verse 7).

The psalmist answers them. “He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?” (verse 9).

Then the psalm grows personal. “Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence” (verse 17). “If I say, ‘My foot is slipping,’ Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me” (verse 18). “When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul” (verse 19).

It ends in trust. “But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The widow, the foreigner and the fatherless had no one to speak for them in court. Israel's law gave them God's own protection. “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:22-23). To kill them was to attack the people God had promised to defend.

Verse 20 asks, ‘Can a corrupt throne be Your ally?’ A ‘throne’ here is a seat of power or judgment. The trouble may be foreign rulers, or Israel's own corrupt courts, ‘mischief by decree’. The psalm does not say which.

The Mishnah lists this as the psalm the Levites sang in the temple on the fourth day of the week.

Verse 9 is clever and simple. The one who made ears must be able to hear. The one who made eyes must be able to see.
passages.later:
Paul writes, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Jesus told of a widow who kept asking a judge for justice, and asked, “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?” (Luke 18:7). Peter writes, “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).
passages.hard: ‘God of vengeance’ (verse 1) can sound like a God of revenge. The book page's part on the cursing psalms explains how Christians read lines like this. Here it is worth seeing what the psalm asks for. It asks the rightful Judge to act when human courts have failed and the weakest are being killed. It hands justice to God and does not take it into its own hands. That is exactly what Paul tells Christians to do in Romans 12:19.
passages.asks:
Who are the widows, foreigners and fatherless in your town? Psalm 94 says God sees how they are treated, even when the powerful think no one is watching.

And if anxiety is overwhelming you (verse 19), you are not alone, and this psalm names it without shame. Bring it to God, who comforts. If worry has become too heavy, tell someone you trust: a friend, a pastor or a doctor.
